title: Gyárfás-Sumner Conjecture
statement_text: For every forest $H$, the class of $H$-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded.
context_text: The Gyárfás-Sumner conjecture [4, 14] is the central backdrop of the paper. The authors work toward a polynomial strengthening, asking which forests $H$ make the class of $H$-free graphs polynomially $\chi$-bounded (i.e., 'good'). The paper establishes polynomial $\chi$-boundedness for $2P_4$-free graphs and more general classes.
paper_contribution: Proves that if $H$ is a good forest then the disjoint union of $H$ and $P_4$ is also good (polynomially $\chi$-bounded), in particular showing that $2P_4$-free graphs satisfy $\chi(G) \leq \omega(G)^{16}$; more generally proves polynomial $\chi$-boundedness for $\{H_1, H_2\}$-free graphs when every component of $H_1$ is good and $H_2$ is a broom or disjoint union of a good forest and paths.

title: Informal Conjecture (every forest is good)
statement_text: Perhaps every forest is good (i.e., for every forest $H$, the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded).
context_text: A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hereditary class (closed under induced subgraphs) is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $f$ with $\chi(G)\le f(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded if $f$ can be taken to be a polynomial; a graph $H$ is good if the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded. The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture asserts that for every forest $H$ the class of $H$-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded; it remains open. Esperet's conjecture that every $\chi$-bounded hereditary class is polynomially $\chi$-bounded was disproved by Briański, Davies and Walczak, so the question is which hereditary classes are polynomially $\chi$-bounded, and in particular whether the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture can be strengthened to polynomial $\chi$-boundedness. The only trees known to be good are those not containing the five-vertex path $P_5$, and it is not known whether $P_5$ is good; it is not even known that a forest whose components are all good is good. The authors prove that if $H$ is a good forest then so is the disjoint union of $H$ and $P_4$ (e.g. $2P_4$-free graphs satisfy $\chi\le\omega^{16}$), and more generally results for disjoint unions of good forests with paths or brooms (a $(k,d)$-broom is a $k$-vertex path with $d$ extra vertices attached to one end).

title: Conjecture 2.3
statement_text: Let $\psi,\sigma:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ be non-decreasing polynomials, let $q\geq 0$ be an integer, and let $H$ be a broom. Then there is a non-decreasing polynomial $\phi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ such that if $G$ is a graph, and $\chi(G)>\phi(\omega(G))$, and $G$ contains no $(\psi,q)$-scattering, then $G$ contains a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of $H$.
context_text: For $X\subseteq V(G)$, $\chi(X)$ and $\omega(X)$ denote $\chi(G[X])$ and $\omega(G[X])$; copies are induced subgraphs; a set is complete (anticomplete) to another if every (no) vertex of the first is adjacent to every vertex of the second. A $(k,d)$-broom is the tree obtained from a $k$-vertex path with one end $v$ by adding $d$ new vertices adjacent to $v$; a broom is a $(k,d)$-broom for some $k,d$. For a non-decreasing $\psi$ and an integer $q\ge0$, a $(\psi,q)$-scattering in $G$ is a triple $(v,P,Q)$ with $P,Q\subseteq V(G)$ disjoint, $v\notin P\cup Q$ complete to $P$ and anticomplete to $Q$, $\chi(P)>\psi(\omega(P))$, and $\chi(Q)>qr+\psi(\omega(Q))$, where $r$ is the maximum over $u\in P$ of the chromatic number of the set of neighbours of $u$ in $Q$. For a non-decreasing $\sigma$, a subgraph $P$ of $G$ is $\sigma$-nondominating if some set $X\subseteq V(G)\setminus V(P)$ anticomplete to $V(P)$ has $\chi(X)>\sigma(\omega(X))$. Excluding scatterings is a weakening of excluding a forest $H_1$ built from good pieces, used to show that unions of good forests with brooms or paths are polynomially $\chi$-bounded ($\chi\le$ a polynomial of $\omega$ on $H$-free graphs). The authors prove the weaker statement in which, under the same hypotheses, $G$ contains a copy of the broom $H$ and a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of a given path $J$; the conjecture asks for a $\sigma$-nondominating copy of the broom itself, an appealing strengthening they could not prove. From the path version they deduce that paths are self-isolating; by the same argument the conjecture would imply that brooms are self-isolating.
